passage.summary: A landowner pays the last hired the same as the first, and asks whether his goodness is a cause for resentment.

context.title: Labourers in the vineyard
paragraphs: Matthew alone records this parable, placed between two sayings about the last being first. [c1] A denarius was the customary pay for a labourer’s day in first-century Palestine. [c2]

The owner’s closing question uses the Jewish idiom of the evil eye, an image for begrudging another’s good fortune. [c3] Matthew has already set the sound eye against the evil eye in the Sermon on the Mount. [c4]

translationNotes.summary: Greek asks “is your eye evil?”, an idiom for begrudging another’s good.
translationNotes.body: The evil eye was a familiar image for stinginess and resentment (Deut 15:9; Prov 28:22). English trades the image for an abstract feeling and loses the echo of Mt 6:22-23. [c3][c4]

translationNotes.summary: The landowner calls himself “good”, not merely “generous”.
translationNotes.body: Agathos is the word Jesus reserves for God in Mt 19:17, a few verses earlier. The parable is about who the owner is, not only what he pays. [c5]

claims.text: The parable of the labourers in the vineyard appears only in Matthew.
A denarius was a usual day’s wage for a labourer.
An “evil eye” was a Jewish idiom for stinginess or begrudging another’s good.
Mt 6:22-23 contrasts the sound eye with the evil eye.
In Mt 19:17 Jesus says that only one is good, using agathos.

segments.title: Labourers in the vineyard
segments.script: Context for Matthew chapter 20, verses 1 to 16. Labourers in the vineyard. Matthew alone records this parable, placed between two sayings about the last being first. A denarius was the customary pay for a labourer’s day in first-century Palestine. The owner’s closing question uses the Jewish idiom of the evil eye, an image for begrudging another’s good fortune. Matthew has already set the sound eye against the evil eye in the Sermon on the Mount.

segments.title: envious · ophthalmos sou ponēros
segments.script: Translation note on Matthew chapter 20, verse 15, the word “envious”. The Greek is ophthalmos sou ponēros, literally “your eye evil”. Greek asks “is your eye evil?”, an idiom for begrudging another’s good. The evil eye was a familiar image for stinginess and resentment (Deuteronomy chapter 15, verse 9; Proverbs chapter 28, verse 22). English trades the image for an abstract feeling and loses the echo of Matthew chapter 6, verses 22 to 23.

segments.title: generous · agathos
segments.script: Translation note on Matthew chapter 20, verse 15, the word “generous”. The Greek is agathos, literally “good”. The landowner calls himself “good”, not merely “generous”. Agathos is the word Jesus reserves for God in Matthew chapter 19, verse 17, a few verses earlier. The parable is about who the owner is, not only what he pays.
